body.heading: A sequence everyone 'knows'
paragraphs: Draw a circle and put points on its edge. Connect every point to every other point with straight lines, and count the regions the circle is cut into. With 1 point there is 1 region. With 2 points, 2 regions. With 3 points, 4 regions. With 4, there are 8. With 5 — draw it carefully — there are 16.
One, two, four, eight, sixteen. The next number is obviously 32. Except it is not. It is 31.

body.heading: Draw it and count
paragraphs: Put 6 points on a circle, spaced as evenly as you can, join every pair, and count the regions one by one, ticking them off on the drawing. You will reach 31 — one region short of the doubling pattern's promise. The sequence was never doubling; it was following a subtler rule that merely agrees with doubling for the first five terms.

This is not a trick played on you. It is a genuine piece of geometry, and it shows something deep: any short list of numbers fits many rules. The first five terms cannot tell you which rule nature — or the puzzle-setter — is using.

body.heading: The lesson
paragraphs: Pattern-spotting is a wonderful instinct, and this puzzle is not a reason to abandon it. It is a reason to hold patterns the right way: as hypotheses to test, not certainties to trust. One more term checked is worth ten terms assumed.

Keep this circle in mind the next time a chart, a headline or a lucky streak shows you four or five points marching in a line. Ask the pattern-spotter's best question: what would the next one look like if I am wrong?

takeaway: Five terms are never a promise — the circle sequence doubles four times, then lands on 31, and checking beats assuming.
